findings.issue_text: [BUG] The import `from sentry.http import safe_urlopen, safe_urlread` pulls these helpers from a module that does not export them — in this repository safe_urlopen/safe_urlread live in sentry.utils.safe_urlopen (sentry/net/http in newer trees), not sentry.http. Importing this module raises ImportError at load time, breaking every request to any GitHub integration endpoint (and the whole control-silo web process that imports it), so the OAuth flow never executes at all.

[BUG] test_github_user_mismatch posts a webhook whose X-Hub-Signature header ('sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486') is the fixture's signature for the original INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE body, but the test mutates webhook_event['sender']['login'] to 'attacker' before posting, so the body no longer matches the declared HMAC. The GitHub webhook view rejects the request with 401/403 on signature verification, the Integration row is never created with sender='attacker', and the subsequent assert resp.status_code == 204 fails — the test cannot pass as written against the real signature check.

[BUG] OAuthLoginView.dispatch calls `get_user_info(payload['access_token'])` and then tests `if 'login' not in authenticated_user_info`, but get_user_info (sentry/identity/github.py) returns None on a GitHub API error rather than raising, so the `in` check runs against None. When GitHub's /user endpoint errors (rate limit, revoked token), `in` on None raises TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable, producing a 500 on the setup endpoint instead of the intended error page returned by error().

[ADVISORY] The tests hardcode the pipeline signature ('9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3' and 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05') as literal strings, coupling the test to the exact md5 of the serialized pipeline state. Any change to PipelineView.signature's inputs (key ordering, added state, serialization detail) silently breaks every one of these tests with an opaque 'Invalid installation request' assertion failure; the next contributor pays a long debugging session to rediscover the coupling.

[ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView.dispatch uses `pipeline.fetch_state('installation_id')` implicitly via bind only when installation_id is in request.GET, but the branch that redirects to GitHub's authorize URL binds state only for this request's pipeline, and the state comparison `request.GET.get('state') != pipeline.signature` assumes the pipeline instance persists across the two round trips with the identical signature — an assumption that breaks if the pipeline is re-instantiated (e.g., due to the session/cache-key layout) between the redirect and the callback. If the pipeline signature is not stable across the authorize round trip (new pipeline object on the callback request fetches a different signature because the saved pipeline state includes the newly-bound installation_id), every legitimate callback is rejected with 'Invalid installation request.' and GitHub setup becomes impossible; the hardcoded-signature tests hide this because they construct both requests in the same test client session.

[BUG] The authenticated-user check indexes integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] without guarding for the sender key, raising KeyError when the Integration row exists without sender metadata. Any GitHub Integration whose metadata was written by a legacy install path, a webhook event that lacked a sender, or an install created before this change now crashes the setup flow with a 500 (unhandled KeyError) instead of the intended error page, when a user in that state completes the OAuth step of the install.

[BUG] get_user_info(payload["access_token"]) is called with no exception handling, so any network error or malformed JSON response from GitHub propagates as an unhandled exception in OAuthLoginView.dispatch. A GitHub outage or transient error on GET /user during the token-exchange step produces a 500 error page mid-install instead of the graceful error() response the surrounding code establishes as the contract for every other failure in this view (bad state, missing token, missing login).

[ADVISORY] The new OAuthLoginView error paths (missing/mismatched state, no code, token exchange returning no access_token) have no test coverage — tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py only exercises the happy token exchange and the user-mismatch path. A future refactor of the state comparison or token parsing (e.g. changing the state source or the parse_qsl handling) will silently break the invalid-request rejection the security enhancement exists to provide; the only test that touches a non-happy OAuth path (test_installation_not_found) conflates several failure modes and asserts only the generic error string.

[ADVISORY] GitHubInstallation now reads installation_id from pipeline state via fetch_state, but OAuthLoginView only binds it when it is present in the initial GET — a user landing on the setup URL without installation_id who then completes OAuth reaches GitHubInstallation with no bound state and only gets silently redirected to the app listing page. Users installing via a flow where GitHub returns only code/state (e.g. the 'install from GitHub' path where installation_id arrives only in the GitHub callback) hit a redirect loop back to the app URL after authenticating, with no error surfaced — the flow fails silently rather than showing the error() page.

[BUG] The new authenticated-user-match invariant is only enforced on the 'Integration exists and is ACTIVE' path; the 'Integration.DoesNotExist' path calls pipeline.next_step() with no user check, so the stated security intent (only the installing GitHub user may complete setup) is not enforced when the webhook that creates the Integration has not yet been processed. An attacker who obtains the installation flow for an app whose Integration record has not yet been created (webhook lag, or webhook dropped) completes the pipeline and links the integration to a Sentry org with no user verification — the exact attack the PR claims to close, since `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` only exists after the webhook lands.

[ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView hand-rolls the entire OAuth leg — state generation/validation, token exchange via safe_urlopen/parse_qsl, and user info fetch — duplicating the existing OAuth2CallbackView / GitHubIdentityProvider machinery rather than reusing it, and the diff even comments 'similar to OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params' / 'similar to OAuth2CallbackView.exchange_token'. Two parallel implementations of GitHub OAuth now exist in the codebase; the next fix to token exchange (e.g. adding PKCE, redirect_uri, error handling for GitHub error payloads) must be applied in both places, and this copy silently diverges — it already omits anything OAuth2CallbackView does beyond the four fields it copies.

[ADVISORY] The diff deletes the FORWARD_INSTALL_FOR constant and inlines the literal "github" into the condition — a refactor unrelated to the stated OAuth security enhancement. Net-zero behavioral change plus one more hardcoded 'github' literal scattered in the codebase; any future work touching the forwarding logic now has one fewer aggregation point. Pure scope churn with no requirement traceability.

[ADVISORY] The error() / get_document_origin() helpers are extracted with a signature change (module-level function taking org, methods dropped) that is broader than the security fix requires, and get_document_origin assumes its argument is always either None or an object with a .organization attribute with no typing or guard. The helper is now callable from anywhere with any truthy non-org value (e.g. an org slug string), raising AttributeError and producing a 500 instead of the rendered error page — the refactor widens the blast radius of a helper whose only purpose was to remove duplication in three render sites.

[ADVISORY] Tests hardcode the pipeline state signature literal '9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3' in six places (and a second signature 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05' in test_installation_not_found) instead of deriving it from the pipeline, indicating the OAuth state has no per-flow entropy the tests rely on. The tests codify that pipeline.signature is a deterministic constant shared across sessions (md5 of a fixed key), meaning the new OAuth 'state' CSRF check validates knowledge of a value derivable from source/config rather than a per-flow nonce — the security property the PR advertises is weaker than the test suite implies, and any change to signature derivation breaks six tests simultaneously.

[ADVISORY] The new ObjectStatus.ACTIVE filter on the second Integration lookup silently changes the semantics of the pre-existing 'Integration exists but has no org link' branch: a non-ACTIVE (disabled/pending-deletion) integration that previously proceeded via pipeline.next_step() now returns the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error. Operators/users re-installing a GitHub app whose Integration row is disabled-but-unlinked get an opaque authenticity-failure message ('We could not verify the authenticity...') for what is actually a status problem, and the previously-supported recovery path (re-link without deleting the row) is removed with no caller update or distinct error message.

[ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView hand-rolls the OAuth2 authorize redirect, token exchange, and response parsing ('similar to OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params / exchange_token' per the code's own comments) instead of reusing the existing OAuth2CallbackView/ProviderPipeline machinery, creating a parallel service path that will drift from the shared implementation. The next fix to the shared token-exchange path (e.g. adding scope validation, error-response handling, or parameter encoding — note the hand-rolled version builds the authorize URL via string concatenation with no urlencode, and drops redirect_uri from the token exchange) will not apply to GitHub's install flow; GitHub users get the bug the fix was for. Deleting this block in favor of the shared callback view removes ~25 lines and one drift site.

[ADVISORY] The state parameter is set to pipeline.signature on the initial redirect and later compared with strict equality against pipeline.signature, but pipeline.signature is not bound to the OAuth request — it is a deterministic function of pipeline state, so the state carries no nonce/freshness and the authorize redirect is issued with no `prompt`/scope parameters and a hand-concatenated query string. Any future pipeline whose serialized state hashes to the same signature (and any replayed callback URL after the flow completed) still passes the state check; the check verifies pipeline ownership, not request freshness, which the error message ('We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request') implies it does. Also the un-urlencoded redirect_uri/state break if either ever contains reserved characters.

[BUG] The previously permissive 'OrganizationIntegration does not exist, but Integration does exist' branch now hard-fails when the Integration row exists with any status other than ObjectStatus.ACTIVE. Before this diff, a user reinstalling a GitHub app whose Integration row exists but is inactive (e.g. disabled) completed setup and proceeded to pipeline.next_step(); now the same request renders 'We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request' — a silent objective change to the existing install flow with no accepted requirement stated for blocking inactive integrations, and the misleading error message gives the user no way to recover except restarting, which hits the same error.

[BUG] The user-match check reads integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] with no guard, so any Integration row whose metadata lacks a 'sender' key raises KeyError. When an Integration for the installation_id was created by a path that does not populate metadata['sender'] (webhook-less creation, older rows created before sender was stored, or org import), the setup request crashes with a 500 KeyError instead of the intended error page or successful install — the security gate meant to return ERR_INTEGRATION_INVALID_INSTALLATION_REQUEST instead takes down the view.

[ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView reuses pipeline.signature as the OAuth 'state' parameter and treats its absence/presence as the discriminator between the pre-authorize and post-authorize legs of the flow. Any caller that reaches the setup URL with a state query param but without completing GitHub's authorize step (e.g. a stale bookmarked callback URL, or GitHub appending state to the initial redirect) is routed into the token-exchange leg with no code, exchanging nothing and rendering the opaque 'Invalid installation request' page — the flow's state contract is implicit and undocumented, so the next maintainer changing pipeline.signature semantics (or adding a state param to any inbound link) silently breaks the discriminator.

[ADVISORY] Multiple tests hard-code the pipeline signature '9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3' (and one a different value 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05' in test_installation_not_found) instead of deriving it from the pipeline. Any change to pipeline signature generation (key rotation, hashing change, org-slug inclusion) breaks five-plus tests with opaque state-mismatch failures that look like product bugs; the two different hard-coded values also reveal the signature is request-dependent, so copy-pasting these blocks into new tests will produce tests that pass for the wrong reason.

[ADVISORY] The OAuth authorize redirect URI is interpolated into a hand-built query string via f-string without URL-encoding. The redirect_uri is currently a plain path so encoding is a no-op today, but any future change that adds query parameters to the setup URL (or a provider_id with reserved characters) produces a malformed authorize URL that GitHub rejects; the code also duplicates hand-rolled query construction that the rest of the codebase builds with urlencode, so the next editor will not know this line is load-bearing on the values being pre-safe.

[BUG] The OAuth `state` anti-CSRF parameter is set to `pipeline.signature`, a deterministic value derived from pipeline state rather than a per-request random nonce, and this same value is then used as the only CSRF check on the callback. The state token is replayable and predictable within a pipeline's lifetime: an attacker who learns or initiates a pipeline can reuse a captured state+code callback pair to complete the OAuth flow in a victim's browser (login-CSRF), binding the attacker-controlled GitHub identity into the victim's org installation flow. A one-time random nonce stored server-side is required; a signature is not a nonce.

[BUG] The authorize redirect URL is built with raw f-string interpolation: `f"{ghip.get_oauth_authorize_url()}?client_id={github_client_id}&state={state}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}"` with redirect_uri unencoded (and state unencoded). absolute_uri can contain characters requiring percent-encoding (query params, fragments, or a path with reserved chars from options-controlled URLs), producing a malformed or attacker-influenceable redirect_uri sent to GitHub; GitHub rejects or misparses the callback URL, breaking the install flow and, with an options-influenced base URL, allowing parameter injection into the authorize endpoint.

[BUG] The authenticated-user check dereferences `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` without checking the key exists, raising KeyError when the integration's metadata lacks a "sender" entry (integrations created by older flows, the API, or webhooks predating sender capture). A user completing setup for an existing ACTIVE integration whose metadata has no sender crashes the request with a KeyError → 500 instead of the rendered error page, on the exact path this diff was written to secure.

[ADVISORY] The token exchange in OAuthLoginView has no CSRF/expiry/replay guard beyond the (signature-derived) state: the returned `code` is exchanged without checking that the pipeline step that initiated the authorize redirect is the same session-bound pipeline step, and a failed exchange swallows all exceptions into an empty payload. An attacker who obtains any valid code+state pair (e.g. via referrer leakage of the GitHub callback URL, which carries both in the query string) can replay it against the setup endpoint within the pipeline's lifetime; broad `except Exception` also hides real failures (network errors, GitHub outage) behind a generic 'could not verify authenticity' message, masking SSRF/connectivity misconfig from operators.

[ADVISORY] The new module-level helper `error` shadows the Python builtin `error` and is defined with mutable-default-adjacent semantics (request/org positional, optional message params), making call sites like `error(request, self.active_organization)` easy to mis-order since the argument is an OrganizationIntegration passed to a parameter named `org`. The next change to error rendering (e.g. adding an org-scoped field) risks passing the wrong object because the parameter name lies about its type; the builtin shadowing also silently changes meaning of any future `error` reference in this module.

[BUG] test_installation_not_found's new assertion `b"Invalid installation request." in resp.content` is satisfied by the OAuthLoginView state-mismatch branch, not by the installation-not-found path the test is named for. The request sends state `ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05` while the same pipeline's valid signature (established in assert_setup_flow for the same org) is `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`, so `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` short-circuits to `error()` and the test passes even if the entire installation-lookup logic below is broken; the removed `"The GitHub installation could not be found."` assertion has no replacement that reaches the Integration lookup at all.

[ADVISORY] The new branch fetching `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` with its DoesNotExist error path, and the `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` lookup, have no test coverage in the diff. Two regressions could ship silently: (1) an integration in a non-ACTIVE status (pending_deletion covered, but e.g. disabled) hits the bare `error(request, self.active_organization)` path that no test executes — a refactor that breaks the ObjectStatus filter would pass the suite; (2) an integration whose `metadata` lacks a `sender` key raises KeyError in `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`, returning a 500 instead of the error page the function promises, and no test creates an integration without sender metadata to catch it.

[ADVISORY] assert_setup_flow hardcodes the full OAuth query string including the pipeline signature hash `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`, and the same literal state is reused across four other tests. The test suite now asserts an exact signature value in five places with no shared constant; when the signature derivation changes (e.g. a pipeline config field is added), all five tests fail with opaque full-string mismatches, and any test that needs a *wrong* state (test_installation_not_found's `ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`) gives no signal that it was intended to be wrong — a future reader 'fixing' it to the canonical hash silently flips which error branch the test exercises.

[BUG] The authenticated-user check does `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` without verifying the `sender` key exists, raising an unhandled KeyError and returning a raw 500 where the `error()` page is the promised contract. Any Integration row whose metadata lacks a `sender` entry (integrations created before this change, or via code paths that never persisted sender from an installation webhook) crashes the setup view with a 500 when a legitimate new organization attempts to link it; the user gets a server error instead of the rendered failure page.

[BUG] `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is called outside any try/except, so any exception it raises (network failure, non-2xx from GitHub's /user endpoint, malformed JSON) propagates as an unhandled 500 instead of the `error()` response the surrounding code returns for every other failure in the view. A transient GitHub outage or a token that GitHub rejects for the /user call turns the OAuth callback into a 500 crash mid-installation, whereas the access-token exchange failure one branch above is carefully caught and rendered as the 'Invalid installation request' page — the token-exchange path is hardened but the immediately following user-info fetch is not.

[ADVISORY] The OAuth code exchange treats all failures identically via a bare `except Exception: payload = {}`, with no logging or metric, so the 'Invalid installation request' page is shown with zero server-side signal distinguishing a misconfigured client_id/secret from a GitHub-side outage or a malformed response. Operators debugging a broken GitHub OAuth app configuration get no log line, no event, and no breadcrumb when the token exchange fails — every diagnostic path routes to the same generic user-facing message; the same swallow also silently discards the GitHub-provided `error`/`error_description` query params GitHub appends to the callback when the user denies authorization, misrepresenting a user denial as an authenticity failure.

[ADVISORY] The `state` anti-CSRF check compares `request.GET.get("state")` to `pipeline.signature` but `pipeline.signature` is used as the OAuth `state` value, and no check verifies that the `code` parameter is present before submitting the token exchange with `code=None`. A callback with a valid state but missing `code` (e.g., GitHub redirecting back on a user-aborted flow while preserving state) causes the server to make a real outbound POST to github.com/login/oauth/access_token with `code=None`, wasting a network round-trip and receiving a guaranteed failure before the generic error page renders — the presence check on `code` should gate the outbound call.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The import `from sentry.http import safe_urlopen, safe_urlread` pulls these helpers from a module that does not export them — in this repository safe_urlopen/safe_urlread live in sentry.utils.safe_urlopen (sentry/net/http in newer trees), not sentry.http. adjudication.rationale: The diff does add `from sentry.http import safe_urlopen, safe_urlread`, but the claim that `sentry.http` does not export these names (and would therefore raise `ImportError`) cannot be verified from the provided diff alone, since it does not include the contents/exports of `sentry/http.py` (or package `sentry/http/__init__.py`). The remainder of the finding (control-silo process breaking, OAuth flow never executing) depends entirely on that unverified import error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] test_github_user_mismatch posts a webhook whose X-Hub-Signature header ('sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486') is the fixture's signature for the original INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE body, but the test mutates webhook_event['sender']['login'] to 'attacker' before posting, so the body no longer matches the declared HMAC. The GitHub webhook view rejects the request with 401/403 on signature verification, the Integration row is never created with sender='attacker', and the subsequent assert resp.status_code == 204 fails — the test cannot pass as written against the real signature check.

adjudication.rationale: In `test_github_user_mismatch`, the test loads `INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE`, mutates the posted JSON body (`webhook_event["sender"]["login"] = "attacker"` and installation id), but still sends a hard-coded `HTTP_X_HUB_SIGNATURE="sha1=d184e..."`. If the webhook endpoint verifies the HMAC against the request body (as GitHub webhooks typically do), this signature would no longer match the mutated payload, causing the webhook request to be rejected and making the subsequent `assert resp.status_code == 204` impossible to satisfy. The diff clearly shows the body mutation without recomputing/updating the signature header.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] OAuthLoginView.dispatch calls `get_user_info(payload['access_token'])` and then tests `if 'login' not in authenticated_user_info`, but get_user_info (sentry/identity/github.py) returns None on a GitHub API error rather than raising, so the `in` check runs against None. When GitHub's /user endpoint errors (rate limit, revoked token), `in` on None raises TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable, producing a 500 on the setup endpoint instead of the intended error page returned by error().

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `OAuthLoginView.dispatch` does `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` and then immediately evaluates `if "login" not in authenticated_user_info:`. This code assumes `get_user_info` returns an iterable/mapping; if it can return `None` or another non-iterable on API failure, the `in` check would raise a `TypeError` and bypass the intended `error()` handling. However, the claimed `get_user_info` behavior (returning `None` on GitHub API error) is not shown in this diff, so the 500 is not strictly verifiable from the provided changes alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The tests hardcode the pipeline signature ('9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3' and 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05') as literal strings, coupling the test to the exact md5 of the serialized pipeline state. Any change to PipelineView.signature's inputs (key ordering, added state, serialization detail) silently breaks every one of these tests with an opaque 'Invalid installation request' assertion failure; the next contributor pays a long debugging session to rediscover the coupling.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows multiple tests asserting or sending literal `state` values like `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` (e.g., `assert_setup_flow`, `test_github_installed_on_another_org`, pending deletion tests) and `ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05` (`test_installation_not_found`). In the new `OAuthLoginView`, `state` is compared against `pipeline.signature` (`if request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature: return error(...)`). This directly couples the tests to the exact signature value/derivation, making them brittle to unrelated signature/serialization changes. That’s a real, diff-grounded maintainability concern but not a functional defect in production code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView.dispatch uses `pipeline.fetch_state('installation_id')` implicitly via bind only when installation_id is in request.GET, but the branch that redirects to GitHub's authorize URL binds state only for this request's pipeline, and the state comparison `request.GET.get('state') != pipeline.signature` assumes the pipeline instance persists across the two round trips with the identical signature — an assumption that breaks if the pipeline is re-instantiated (e.g., due to the session/cache-key layout) between the redirect and the callback. If the pipeline signature is not stable across the authorize round trip (new pipeline object on the callback request fetches a different signature because the saved pipeline state includes the newly-bound installation_id), every legitimate callback is rejected with 'Invalid installation request.' and GitHub setup becomes impossible; the hardcoded-signature tests hide this because they construct both requests in the same test client session.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `installation_id` is bound to the pipeline *before* `state = pipeline.signature` is computed in `OAuthLoginView.dispatch` (so if the signature depends on bound state, the outgoing `state` would already reflect it). On the callback request, the code compares `request.GET['state']` to `pipeline.signature`, but nothing in the diff indicates `pipeline.signature` is unstable across requests or recomputed from different inputs when the pipeline is reloaded. The finding’s core claim (signature changes because `installation_id` gets newly bound after the first round trip / pipeline re-instantiation) is not supported by the code shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The authenticated-user check indexes integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] without guarding for the sender key, raising KeyError when the Integration row exists without sender metadata. Any GitHub Integration whose metadata was written by a legacy install path, a webhook event that lacked a sender, or an install created before this change now crashes the setup flow with a 500 (unhandled KeyError) instead of the intended error page, when a user in that state completes the OAuth step of the install.

[BUG] get_user_info(payload["access_token"]) is called with no exception handling, so any network error or malformed JSON response from GitHub propagates as an unhandled exception in OAuthLoginView.dispatch. A GitHub outage or transient error on GET /user during the token-exchange step produces a 500 error page mid-install instead of the graceful error() response the surrounding code establishes as the contract for every other failure in this view (bad state, missing token, missing login).

adjudication.rationale: In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, after verifying `access_token` exists, the code calls `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` and then checks for a `login` key. Unlike the earlier token parsing (wrapped in `try/except`), this call is not wrapped in any exception handling. Since `get_user_info` is newly imported from `sentry.identity.github` and is used to fetch GitHub user data, any exception it raises (e.g., request failure/timeout, non-JSON/malformed response parsing) would propagate and result in an unhandled 500 instead of returning the `error()` response that the view otherwise uses for failure cases.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new OAuthLoginView error paths (missing/mismatched state, no code, token exchange returning no access_token) have no test coverage — tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py only exercises the happy token exchange and the user-mismatch path. A future refactor of the state comparison or token parsing (e.g. changing the state source or the parse_qsl handling) will silently break the invalid-request rejection the security enhancement exists to provide; the only test that touches a non-happy OAuth path (test_installation_not_found) conflates several failure modes and asserts only the generic error string.

adjudication.rationale: OAuthLoginView introduces several new rejection branches that are not specifically covered by tests: it returns `error(...)` on state mismatch (`if request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`), on missing/invalid token response (`if "access_token" not in payload` after `parse_qsl`), and on missing `login` from `get_user_info`. The updated tests primarily cover the happy authorize→token→/user flow (`assert_setup_flow`) and the post-install “github user mismatch” check in `GitHubInstallation`. While `test_installation_not_found` does exercise one OAuth failure (state mismatch) by asserting the generic "Invalid installation request.", it does not isolate/cover the other OAuth error paths (e.g., no `code`, token exchange returning no `access_token`, malformed body/parse failure), so regressions in those branches could slip through.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] GitHubInstallation now reads installation_id from pipeline state via fetch_state, but OAuthLoginView only binds it when it is present in the initial GET — a user landing on the setup URL without installation_id who then completes OAuth reaches GitHubInstallation with no bound state and only gets silently redirected to the app listing page. Users installing via a flow where GitHub returns only code/state (e.g. the 'install from GitHub' path where installation_id arrives only in the GitHub callback) hit a redirect loop back to the app URL after authenticating, with no error surfaced — the flow fails silently rather than showing the error() page.

adjudication.rationale: In the new flow, hitting the setup URL without an `installation_id` intentionally triggers OAuth first; after successful OAuth, the pipeline advances to `GitHubInstallation`, which (when still missing `installation_id`) redirects to the GitHub App URL (`/apps/...`) so the user can install and then return with `installation_id`. This behavior is exercised in `assert_setup_flow`: OAuth callback (code/state only) leads to a redirect to `/apps/sentry-test-app`, and only later does the test hit the setup URL with `installation_id`. Also, the “install from GitHub without pipeline” case is handled in `pipeline_advancer.py` when `setup_action=install` and `pipeline is None`. The finding’s claimed silent failure/loop isn’t supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new authenticated-user-match invariant is only enforced on the 'Integration exists and is ACTIVE' path; the 'Integration.DoesNotExist' path calls pipeline.next_step() with no user check, so the stated security intent (only the installing GitHub user may complete setup) is not enforced when the webhook that creates the Integration has not yet been processed. An attacker who obtains the installation flow for an app whose Integration record has not yet been created (webhook lag, or webhook dropped) completes the pipeline and links the integration to a Sentry org with no user verification — the exact attack the PR claims to close, since `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` only exists after the webhook lands.

adjudication.rationale: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, the user-match check against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` is only executed in the branch where an ACTIVE `Integration` is successfully fetched (after the `installations_exist` check). If `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `Integration.DoesNotExist`, the code immediately does `return pipeline.next_step()` (see the `except Integration.DoesNotExist:` block around the `installations_exist` query) with no verification of `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")`. Since `github_authenticated_user` is only compared to `integration.metadata` later (and that metadata is only available once an Integration exists, typically after webhook processing), the stated authenticated-user invariant is not enforced on the 'integration not yet created' path shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView hand-rolls the entire OAuth leg — state generation/validation, token exchange via safe_urlopen/parse_qsl, and user info fetch — duplicating the existing OAuth2CallbackView / GitHubIdentityProvider machinery rather than reusing it, and the diff even comments 'similar to OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params' / 'similar to OAuth2CallbackView.exchange_token'. Two parallel implementations of GitHub OAuth now exist in the codebase; the next fix to token exchange (e.g. adding PKCE, redirect_uri, error handling for GitHub error payloads) must be applied in both places, and this copy silently diverges — it already omits anything OAuth2CallbackView does beyond the four fields it copies.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly introduces a new `OAuthLoginView` that manually implements OAuth callback behavior: it generates/validates `state` (`state = pipeline.signature`, compares `request.GET.get("state")`), exchanges the code for a token via `safe_urlopen`/`safe_urlread` and `parse_qsl`, and then calls `get_user_info(access_token)` to fetch the GitHub login. The code itself explicitly notes it is "similar to OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params" and "similar to OAuth2CallbackView.exchange_token", indicating duplication rather than reuse of existing OAuth machinery. This is a concrete maintainability/architecture concern introduced by the change (two parallel OAuth flows that can diverge), but it is not, by itself, a directly verifiable functional defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The diff deletes the FORWARD_INSTALL_FOR constant and inlines the literal "github" into the condition — a refactor unrelated to the stated OAuth security enhancement. Net-zero behavioral change plus one more hardcoded 'github' literal scattered in the codebase; any future work touching the forwarding logic now has one fewer aggregation point. Pure scope churn with no requirement traceability.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does remove `FORWARD_INSTALL_FOR = ["github"]` and replaces `provider_id in FORWARD_INSTALL_FOR` with `provider_id == "github"` in `pipeline_advancer.py`, which is a net-zero behavior change. However, calling this out as a review “issue” is essentially a minor refactor/style preference (constant vs inline literal) rather than a concrete defect or an important, actionable problem created by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The error() / get_document_origin() helpers are extracted with a signature change (module-level function taking org, methods dropped) that is broader than the security fix requires, and get_document_origin assumes its argument is always either None or an object with a .organization attribute with no typing or guard. The helper is now callable from anywhere with any truthy non-org value (e.g. an org slug string), raising AttributeError and producing a 500 instead of the rendered error page — the refactor widens the blast radius of a helper whose only purpose was to remove duplication in three render sites.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce new module-level helpers `error(request, org, ...)` and `get_document_origin(org)` (with no type annotation on `org`) and `get_document_origin` unconditionally dereferences `org.organization` when `org` is truthy. That means the helper is not defensive against being passed the wrong kind of value and could raise `AttributeError` if misused. However, in this diff all call sites pass `self.active_organization` (previously used the same `.organization` access inline), so there’s no verifiable new 500 in the shown behavior; the concern is primarily about broadened surface area / future misuse rather than a demonstrated defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Tests hardcode the pipeline state signature literal '9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3' in six places (and a second signature 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05' in test_installation_not_found) instead of deriving it from the pipeline, indicating the OAuth state has no per-flow entropy the tests rely on. The tests codify that pipeline.signature is a deterministic constant shared across sessions (md5 of a fixed key), meaning the new OAuth 'state' CSRF check validates knowledge of a value derivable from source/config rather than a per-flow nonce — the security property the PR advertises is weaker than the test suite implies, and any change to signature derivation breaks six tests simultaneously.

[ADVISORY] The new ObjectStatus.ACTIVE filter on the second Integration lookup silently changes the semantics of the pre-existing 'Integration exists but has no org link' branch: a non-ACTIVE (disabled/pending-deletion) integration that previously proceeded via pipeline.next_step() now returns the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error. Operators/users re-installing a GitHub app whose Integration row is disabled-but-unlinked get an opaque authenticity-failure message ('We could not verify the authenticity...') for what is actually a status problem, and the previously-supported recovery path (re-link without deleting the row) is removed with no caller update or distinct error message.

adjudication.rationale: Diff verifiably changes behavior in `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`: previously, when an `Integration` existed but had no `OrganizationIntegration` link (`installations_exist` is False), the code always did `pipeline.next_step()` (after binding `installation_id`). Now it performs a second lookup requiring `status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE` and otherwise returns the generic `error(... ERR_INTEGRATION_INVALID_INSTALLATION_REQUEST ...)`. This means a non-ACTIVE (e.g., disabled) unlinked Integration that would previously proceed is now blocked with an “authenticity” failure message. Whether that’s a true defect vs intended tightening isn’t provable from the diff alone, but the semantic/UX change is real and review-relevant.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView hand-rolls the OAuth2 authorize redirect, token exchange, and response parsing ('similar to OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params / exchange_token' per the code's own comments) instead of reusing the existing OAuth2CallbackView/ProviderPipeline machinery, creating a parallel service path that will drift from the shared implementation. The next fix to the shared token-exchange path (e.g. adding scope validation, error-response handling, or parameter encoding — note the hand-rolled version builds the authorize URL via string concatenation with no urlencode, and drops redirect_uri from the token exchange) will not apply to GitHub's install flow; GitHub users get the bug the fix was for. Deleting this block in favor of the shared callback view removes ~25 lines and one drift site.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `OAuthLoginView` that manually constructs the GitHub authorize URL via f-string concatenation (`...?client_id=...&state=...&redirect_uri=...`) and manually exchanges/parses the access token response using `safe_urlopen` + `parse_qsl`, with comments explicitly noting it is “similar to OAuth2CallbackView...”. This creates a separate OAuth/token-exchange implementation path that can drift from any shared/oauth2 callback machinery elsewhere. While the diff does not prove an immediate functional break for GitHub, it is a concrete, diff-grounded maintainability/architecture concern introduced by this change (e.g., no centralized error handling/encoding behavior).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The state parameter is set to pipeline.signature on the initial redirect and later compared with strict equality against pipeline.signature, but pipeline.signature is not bound to the OAuth request — it is a deterministic function of pipeline state, so the state carries no nonce/freshness and the authorize redirect is issued with no `prompt`/scope parameters and a hand-concatenated query string. Any future pipeline whose serialized state hashes to the same signature (and any replayed callback URL after the flow completed) still passes the state check; the check verifies pipeline ownership, not request freshness, which the error message ('We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request') implies it does. Also the un-urlencoded redirect_uri/state break if either ever contains reserved characters.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `OAuthLoginView` constructing the GitHub authorize URL by hand with an f-string (`...?client_id=...&state=...&redirect_uri=...`) rather than using proper URL encoding, so if `redirect_uri`/`state` ever contain reserved characters this could break (even if they currently look safe). The view also uses `state = pipeline.signature` and later checks `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`, which (as written) only proves the callback matches the current pipeline identifier; the diff does not show any separate per-request nonce/freshness binding. However, whether `pipeline.signature` is deterministic/replayable cannot be verified from this diff alone, so treating it as a definite security bug is not fully supportable from the patch context.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The previously permissive 'OrganizationIntegration does not exist, but Integration does exist' branch now hard-fails when the Integration row exists with any status other than ObjectStatus.ACTIVE. Before this diff, a user reinstalling a GitHub app whose Integration row exists but is inactive (e.g. disabled) completed setup and proceeded to pipeline.next_step(); now the same request renders 'We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request' — a silent objective change to the existing install flow with no accepted requirement stated for blocking inactive integrations, and the misleading error message gives the user no way to recover except restarting, which hits the same error.

adjudication.rationale: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, the branch comment "OrganizationIntegration does not exist, but Integration does exist." previously unconditionally did `pipeline.next_step()` after binding `installation_id`. The diff now adds `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` and returns `error(...)` on `DoesNotExist`. This makes setups fail for existing `Integration` rows in any non-ACTIVE status (e.g., DISABLED), a behavioral regression that is directly visible in the diff and produces the generic "Invalid installation request" error with no alternate recovery path shown in this code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The user-match check reads integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] with no guard, so any Integration row whose metadata lacks a 'sender' key raises KeyError. When an Integration for the installation_id was created by a path that does not populate metadata['sender'] (webhook-less creation, older rows created before sender was stored, or org import), the setup request crashes with a 500 KeyError instead of the intended error page or successful install — the security gate meant to return ERR_INTEGRATION_INVALID_INSTALLATION_REQUEST instead takes down the view.

[ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView reuses pipeline.signature as the OAuth 'state' parameter and treats its absence/presence as the discriminator between the pre-authorize and post-authorize legs of the flow. Any caller that reaches the setup URL with a state query param but without completing GitHub's authorize step (e.g. a stale bookmarked callback URL, or GitHub appending state to the initial redirect) is routed into the token-exchange leg with no code, exchanging nothing and rendering the opaque 'Invalid installation request' page — the flow's state contract is implicit and undocumented, so the next maintainer changing pipeline.signature semantics (or adding a state param to any inbound link) silently breaks the discriminator.

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows OAuthLoginView uses `pipeline.signature` as OAuth `state` and uses only presence/absence of `request.GET.get("state")` to decide between redirect-to-authorize vs callback handling. If a request hits `/extensions/github/setup/` with a `state` query param but no `code`, the view will proceed into the token-exchange branch (`data = {"code": request.GET.get("code"), ...}`), call `safe_urlopen(...)`, and then render the generic `error(...)` page when `access_token` is missing. That behavior is real but it’s an edge-case/maintainability concern rather than a clearly verifiable defect from the diff (it fails closed with an error page, not an insecure bypass).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Multiple tests hard-code the pipeline signature '9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3' (and one a different value 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05' in test_installation_not_found) instead of deriving it from the pipeline. Any change to pipeline signature generation (key rotation, hashing change, org-slug inclusion) breaks five-plus tests with opaque state-mismatch failures that look like product bugs; the two different hard-coded values also reveal the signature is request-dependent, so copy-pasting these blocks into new tests will produce tests that pass for the wrong reason.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows multiple tests hard-coding the OAuth `state`/pipeline signature value (e.g. `state=9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` asserted in `assert_setup_flow` and reused in several tests, and `ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05` used in `test_installation_not_found`). In the new `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, the callback rejects when `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` and returns the generic `error(...)`. This makes tests brittle to any change in how `pipeline.signature` is generated; it’s a maintainability/test-robustness issue rather than a runtime product defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The OAuth authorize redirect URI is interpolated into a hand-built query string via f-string without URL-encoding. The redirect_uri is currently a plain path so encoding is a no-op today, but any future change that adds query parameters to the setup URL (or a provider_id with reserved characters) produces a malformed authorize URL that GitHub rejects; the code also duplicates hand-rolled query construction that the rest of the codebase builds with urlencode, so the next editor will not know this line is load-bearing on the values being pre-safe.

adjudication.rationale: In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, the GitHub authorize URL is constructed via an f-string: `...authorize_url()?client_id=...&state=...&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}`. The diff shows `redirect_uri` is produced by `absolute_uri(reverse(...))` and is not URL-encoded or assembled via `urlencode`, unlike other places in the codebase/tests that use `urlencode(...)`. Today `reverse(...)` returns a plain path (`/extensions/github/setup/`), so it likely works, but the review point is valid as a robustness/maintainability issue: if `redirect_uri` ever includes query params or reserved characters, the hand-built query string could become malformed and be rejected by GitHub.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The OAuth `state` anti-CSRF parameter is set to `pipeline.signature`, a deterministic value derived from pipeline state rather than a per-request random nonce, and this same value is then used as the only CSRF check on the callback. The state token is replayable and predictable within a pipeline's lifetime: an attacker who learns or initiates a pipeline can reuse a captured state+code callback pair to complete the OAuth flow in a victim's browser (login-CSRF), binding the attacker-controlled GitHub identity into the victim's org installation flow. A one-time random nonce stored server-side is required; a signature is not a nonce.
matched_golden_ids: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate issue describes that OAuth `state` is set to `pipeline.signature`, a deterministic/static value, instead of a per-request random nonce, making it predictable/replayable and weakening CSRF protection. This is the same underlying issue as the golden comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The authorize redirect URL is built with raw f-string interpolation: `f"{ghip.get_oauth_authorize_url()}?client_id={github_client_id}&state={state}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}"` with redirect_uri unencoded (and state unencoded). absolute_uri can contain characters requiring percent-encoding (query params, fragments, or a path with reserved chars from options-controlled URLs), producing a malformed or attacker-influenceable redirect_uri sent to GitHub; GitHub rejects or misparses the callback URL, breaking the install flow and, with an options-influenced base URL, allowing parameter injection into the authorize endpoint.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does build the GitHub authorize URL via raw f-string concatenation in `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, inserting `state` and `redirect_uri` without `urlencode`/percent-encoding. However, in this change `redirect_uri` is produced as `absolute_uri(reverse(...))` (a fixed path with no query/fragment), and the added test asserts the unencoded query string exactly, indicating this is expected to work as-is. The finding’s stronger claims about malformed URLs/attacker parameter injection aren’t directly supported by the diff, but using proper encoding would still be a concrete hardening/robustness improvement grounded in the shown code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The authenticated-user check dereferences `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` without checking the key exists, raising KeyError when the integration's metadata lacks a "sender" entry (integrations created by older flows, the API, or webhooks predating sender capture). A user completing setup for an existing ACTIVE integration whose metadata has no sender crashes the request with a KeyError → 500 instead of the rendered error page, on the exact path this diff was written to secure.
matched_golden_ids: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same bug: the code accesses integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] (or equivalent) without verifying the "sender" key exists in metadata, leading to a KeyError for integrations created without sender metadata.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The token exchange in OAuthLoginView has no CSRF/expiry/replay guard beyond the (signature-derived) state: the returned `code` is exchanged without checking that the pipeline step that initiated the authorize redirect is the same session-bound pipeline step, and a failed exchange swallows all exceptions into an empty payload. An attacker who obtains any valid code+state pair (e.g. via referrer leakage of the GitHub callback URL, which carries both in the query string) can replay it against the setup endpoint within the pipeline's lifetime; broad `except Exception` also hides real failures (network errors, GitHub outage) behind a generic 'could not verify authenticity' message, masking SSRF/connectivity misconfig from operators.

adjudication.rationale: Diff adds OAuthLoginView that uses only `state == pipeline.signature` as its integrity check and does not add any explicit expiry/one-time-use guard for the OAuth callback beyond that comparison. However, whether this enables replay/CSRF depends on how `pipeline.signature` is generated/bound (not shown in the diff) and on GitHub OAuth code one-time semantics, so the exploitability claim isn’t directly verifiable here. What is directly grounded: the token exchange response parsing wraps `safe_urlread(req)` / `parse_qsl` in a broad `except Exception:` and collapses all parse/decoding errors into `payload = {}` (then returns a generic `error(...)`), which can obscure real response/format issues and makes debugging harder.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new module-level helper `error` shadows the Python builtin `error` and is defined with mutable-default-adjacent semantics (request/org positional, optional message params), making call sites like `error(request, self.active_organization)` easy to mis-order since the argument is an OrganizationIntegration passed to a parameter named `org`. The next change to error rendering (e.g. adding an org-scoped field) risks passing the wrong object because the parameter name lies about its type; the builtin shadowing also silently changes meaning of any future `error` reference in this module.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a module-level function named `error(...)`, but this does not actually shadow a Python builtin (there is no builtin named `error`). The rest of the finding is speculative maintainability/style commentary: `error(request, self.active_organization)` is consistent with how `get_document_origin(org)` uses `org.organization`, and the diff shows no mis-ordering or type mismatch bug at call sites. No verifiable defect or concrete diff-grounded issue is demonstrated.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] test_installation_not_found's new assertion `b"Invalid installation request." in resp.content` is satisfied by the OAuthLoginView state-mismatch branch, not by the installation-not-found path the test is named for. The request sends state `ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05` while the same pipeline's valid signature (established in assert_setup_flow for the same org) is `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`, so `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` short-circuits to `error()` and the test passes even if the entire installation-lookup logic below is broken; the removed `"The GitHub installation could not be found."` assertion has no replacement that reaches the Integration lookup at all.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `OAuthLoginView.dispatch` returns `error(...)` when `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`, before any installation lookup in `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`. In `test_installation_not_found`, the new request uses `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"` and then asserts `b"Invalid installation request." in resp.content`, which can be satisfied by that state-mismatch branch without exercising the intended "installation not found" behavior. Since this is a test-coverage/accuracy issue (the test no longer validates the installation-lookup path) rather than a demonstrated production behavior defect, it fits better as an important non-bug review issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new branch fetching `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` with its DoesNotExist error path, and the `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` lookup, have no test coverage in the diff. Two regressions could ship silently: (1) an integration in a non-ACTIVE status (pending_deletion covered, but e.g. disabled) hits the bare `error(request, self.active_organization)` path that no test executes — a refactor that breaks the ObjectStatus filter would pass the suite; (2) an integration whose `metadata` lacks a `sender` key raises KeyError in `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`, returning a 500 instead of the error page the function promises, and no test creates an integration without sender metadata to catch it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new logic in `GitHubInstallation.dispatch` that can return `error(...)` when `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` fails, and it directly indexes `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` without guarding against missing keys. The added tests do exercise the sender/login lookup in the mismatch case (`test_github_user_mismatch` sets `webhook_event["sender"]["login"] = "attacker"`), so the finding’s claim of *no* coverage for that lookup is overstated. However, there is still no test for (a) an existing integration with a non-ACTIVE status hitting the `DoesNotExist` -> `error(...)` path, and (b) an integration whose `metadata` lacks `sender` (which would raise `KeyError` and 500). These are specific, diff-grounded gaps/edge cases rather than a proven defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] assert_setup_flow hardcodes the full OAuth query string including the pipeline signature hash `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`, and the same literal state is reused across four other tests. The test suite now asserts an exact signature value in five places with no shared constant; when the signature derivation changes (e.g. a pipeline config field is added), all five tests fail with opaque full-string mismatches, and any test that needs a *wrong* state (test_installation_not_found's `ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`) gives no signal that it was intended to be wrong — a future reader 'fixing' it to the canonical hash silently flips which error branch the test exercises.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows multiple tests hardcoding the exact OAuth `state` value `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` (e.g., `assert_setup_flow` asserts the full `redirect.query` string with that literal state, and other tests build `setup_path_2` with the same literal). `test_installation_not_found` uses a different hardcoded state (`ddd023...`) to trigger the invalid-request branch. This is a real test-maintainability/brittleness issue introduced by the change: if `pipeline.signature` derivation changes, several tests will fail with opaque full-query mismatches, and the “wrong state” test doesn’t document intent via a shared constant/helper.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The authenticated-user check does `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` without verifying the `sender` key exists, raising an unhandled KeyError and returning a raw 500 where the `error()` page is the promised contract. Any Integration row whose metadata lacks a `sender` entry (integrations created before this change, or via code paths that never persisted sender from an installation webhook) crashes the setup view with a 500 when a legitimate new organization attempts to link it; the user gets a server error instead of the rendered failure page.

adjudication.rationale: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, the new authenticated-user verification compares against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` without guarding for missing keys (`sender`/`login`). If an existing `Integration` row has metadata that doesn’t include `sender` (or lacks `login`), this will raise a `KeyError` and produce an unhandled 500 instead of returning the `error()` failure page that this flow otherwise uses.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is called outside any try/except, so any exception it raises (network failure, non-2xx from GitHub's /user endpoint, malformed JSON) propagates as an unhandled 500 instead of the `error()` response the surrounding code returns for every other failure in the view. A transient GitHub outage or a token that GitHub rejects for the /user call turns the OAuth callback into a 500 crash mid-installation, whereas the access-token exchange failure one branch above is carefully caught and rendered as the 'Invalid installation request' page — the token-exchange path is hardened but the immediately following user-info fetch is not.

adjudication.rationale: In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, the OAuth callback path wraps `safe_urlread(...); payload = dict(parse_qsl(body))` in a try/except and returns `error(...)` on failure, but the subsequent call `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is not inside any try/except. Any exception from `get_user_info` (e.g., network/HTTP/parse errors) would propagate and result in an unhandled 500 rather than the intended `error()` page, making the flow less robust than the preceding token-exchange logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The OAuth code exchange treats all failures identically via a bare `except Exception: payload = {}`, with no logging or metric, so the 'Invalid installation request' page is shown with zero server-side signal distinguishing a misconfigured client_id/secret from a GitHub-side outage or a malformed response. Operators debugging a broken GitHub OAuth app configuration get no log line, no event, and no breadcrumb when the token exchange fails — every diagnostic path routes to the same generic user-facing message; the same swallow also silently discards the GitHub-provided `error`/`error_description` query params GitHub appends to the callback when the user denies authorization, misrepresenting a user denial as an authenticity failure.

adjudication.rationale: In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, the token exchange parses the response in a broad `try/except Exception` and on any exception sets `payload = {}` (no logging/metrics) before falling back to `return error(...)` when `access_token` is missing. This is visible in the new code around `body = safe_urlread(req).decode(...)` / `payload = dict(parse_qsl(body))`. The view also does not branch on GitHub callback parameters like `error`/`error_description` (it only checks `state` and then proceeds to exchange `code`), so a denial or other OAuth error will be surfaced as the same generic "Invalid installation request" page. These are concrete, diff-grounded observability/UX shortcomings, but not a strictly verifiable functional break given the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The `state` anti-CSRF check compares `request.GET.get("state")` to `pipeline.signature` but `pipeline.signature` is used as the OAuth `state` value, and no check verifies that the `code` parameter is present before submitting the token exchange with `code=None`. A callback with a valid state but missing `code` (e.g., GitHub redirecting back on a user-aborted flow while preserving state) causes the server to make a real outbound POST to github.com/login/oauth/access_token with `code=None`, wasting a network round-trip and receiving a guaranteed failure before the generic error page renders — the presence check on `code` should gate the outbound call.

adjudication.rationale: In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, after verifying `request.GET.get("state") == pipeline.signature`, it unconditionally builds `data` with `"code": request.GET.get("code")` and immediately calls `safe_urlopen(url=..., data=data)` to exchange the token. There is no guard that `code` is present/non-empty before making the outbound POST. Therefore a callback URL with a valid `state` but missing `code` will still trigger a real network request to `https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` (with `code=None`), and only then fall through to the generic error when `access_token` is absent. This is a concrete, diff-shown behavior and should be gated by checking `code` first.
